sections.heading: Welcome to continuous revenue
sections.subheading: The quarter-end scramble was the operating model. It ends here.

sections.heading: The old model is the competitor
sections.body:
Revenue teams still run on a model built for annual planning cycles: forecast at the start, scramble at the end, reconcile in between.

Continuous revenue replaces the cycle with a loop — every signal lands in the plan the day it happens, and the plan re-forecasts itself. Not a dashboard over the old model. A different model.

pages.meta_description: Continuous revenue, defined — the essay behind the category.

sections.heading: Continuous revenue, defined
sections.subheading: The essay behind the category — what broke, and what replaces it.

sections.body:
Quarterly revenue planning made sense when signals arrived quarterly. They don't anymore.

Every buyer touch is observable the moment it happens — yet most teams still batch them into a quarterly reconciliation, then scramble when the batch disagrees with the plan. The scramble isn't a discipline problem. It's the operating model working as designed.

Continuous revenue is the replacement model: the plan is a running system that consumes every signal on arrival and re-forecasts itself, with a named human approving every move the system proposes. Continuous, because the loop never batches. Revenue, because the loop owns the number.

A continuous revenue system has three properties: it reacts to signals the day they happen, it shows the lineage behind every number, and it never acts outward without a human's name on the action.

bullets.title: The Monday forecast meeting becomes a review, not an argument

items.a: Forecasting tools predict the number under the old model. Continuous revenue changes when and how the number moves — the model, not the math.

items.q: Isn't a new category just marketing?
items.a: Judge it by the properties: signal-driven re-forecasting, full lineage, named approvals. If a tool has all three, it's running the model — whatever it's called.
Start with one pipeline. The model proves itself in a quarter or it doesn't.
